summary: Background: Frailty is prevalent among hospitalized patients and is associated with increased risk of complications, prolonged hospitalization, higher mortality, and health care costs. Existing frailty screening tools, including the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and Hospital Frailty Risk Score (HFRS), have limitations related to subjectivity, resource intensity, or reliance on retrospective data, limiting their use in routine acute care. Early identification of frailty is critical to support targeted interventions and resource allocation, yet scalable approaches for predicting frailty early during hospital admission remain limited. Objective: This paper evaluates whether routinely collected electronic medical record (EMR) data available within the first 72 hours of admission can be used to predict frailty in hospitalized patients. Methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted using routinely collected EMR data from the Royal Adelaide Hospital (RAH), including overnight admissions with a length of stay of at least 72 hours between July 2023 and December 2024. Frailty was defined using the HFRS (score >4). Predictors were derived from EMR data available within 72 hours of admission, including demographics, medications, laboratory results, nursing assessments, and medical and allied health consult orders. Data were split into training (21,436/26,824, 80%) and test (5388/26,824, 20%) sets. Multiple machine learning models were trained, with the -score as the primary optimization metric. Model performance was evaluated using the -score, recall, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), calibration, and clinical utility analyses. Results: This study included 26,824 admissions, of whom 9427 (35%) were classified as frail. The final XGBoost (XGB) model achieved an -score of 0.755 (95% CI 0.741-0.768), an AUROC of 0.777 (95% CI 0.764-0.790), and a recall of 0.873 (95% CI 0.857-0.887) on the test dataset, with good calibration and an expected-to-observed ratio close to 1 (0.996, 95% CI 0.963-1.028). Key predictors included polypharmacy, laboratory results (including creatinine, albumin, and sodium), allied health consult orders, and nursing assessment data. Model performance was lower at 24 hours postadmission and improved by discharge. Conclusions: An EMR-based frailty prediction model using data available at 72 hours postadmission can identify patients with frailty early in their hospital stay, supporting targeted interventions and operational planning. Reduced performance in Indigenous patients highlights the need for culturally validated frailty indices and ongoing evaluation of equity in predictive modeling.
title: Development and Internal Validation of an Electronic Medical Record–Based Machine Learning Model for Frailty Prediction in Hospitalized Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: Background: Schizophrenia is a severe mental disorder characterized by high disability and relapse rates, posing significant challenges to public safety and community-based mental health management. Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate a model for identifying hospitalization-related severe relapse risk among individuals with schizophrenia and to determine the key factors associated with this risk. Methods: A total of 44,804 electronic records of community-managed individuals with schizophrenia were extracted from an information management system between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2023. The dataset included demographic information, clinical records, interview data, policy support, and management indicators to construct a comprehensive feature system. A Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) machine learning algorithm was used for model development, with cost-sensitive learning applied to address class imbalance. Model interpretability was enhanced using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to identify the most influential predictors of relapse risk. Results: After screening, a total of 39,818 community-dwelling individuals with schizophrenia were included in this study, of whom 3717 (9.33%) experienced hospitalization-related severe relapse. The dataset was randomly divided using stratified sampling into a training set (n=31,854, 80%) and an independent test set (n=7964, 20%). Among the 6 machine learning models evaluated, LightGBM showed leading and balanced performance, yielding an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.95, an area under the precision–recall curve of 0.79, a relapse-class recall of 0.77, a precision of 0.71, and an -score of 0.74 in the independent test set. SHAP-based interpretability analysis identified medication persistence (23.30%), specialist recommendation: medication adherence training (19.74%), number of follow-ups (7.38%), age (3.72%), and educational attainment (3.58%) as the most influential predictors. Higher hospitalization-related severe relapse risk was generally associated with interrupted or refused medication use, more frequent follow-ups, younger age, and higher educational attainment, whereas sustained medication use, better occupational functioning and productive work, greater social participation, and better social functioning were associated with lower predicted risk. Conclusions: This study developed a hospitalization-related severe relapse risk identification model that integrates multidimensional factors reflecting the clinical and functional complexity of schizophrenia. The findings provide an evidence-based foundation for risk identification, targeted intervention, and the optimization of community mental health services to reduce hospitalization-related severe relapse risk and support long-term recovery.
title: Analysis and Prediction of Relapse Risk Factors in Community-Dwelling Individuals With Schizophrenia: Retrospective Cohort Study

summary: Background: The rapid rise of secure patient messaging has transformed ophthalmic communication, with text volumes now exceeding prepandemic levels across health care systems. Our study uses a natural language processing (NLP) model to explore patterns in over 30,000 secure messages and identify common ocular complaints and differences by patient demographics. Objective: The objective of this study is to characterize the clinical and administrative concerns communicated through secure ophthalmology messaging and to assess differences in message content across patient sociodemographic groups. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study of deidentified, patient-initiated secure messages sent between June 2014 and July 2024. Patients with ophthalmic conditions who initiated secure electronic health record (EHR) portal messages were included. Of the 52,388 extracted message threads, 30,390 (58%) patient medical advice request (PMAR) messages routed solely to the Department of Ophthalmology from 4817 unique patients were assessed after the exclusion of questionnaires, courtesy messages, clinician responses, and messages routed to other health care departments. Of these unique patients, 2673 (55.5%) were female, 2740 (56.9%) were aged 50 years or older, 2346 (48.7%) were White, 4392 (91.2%) were non-Hispanic, and 2774 (57.6%) were married. NLP and large language model (LLM)–assisted topic classification were used to categorize message content. The distribution of message topics and frequency of clinical concerns were assessed and stratified by age, sex, race, ethnicity, and marital status. Differences in message frequency by demographic subgroup were assessed using 2-proportion z-tests. Results: Following preprocessing and topic modeling, 14,284 (47%) of the 30,390 messages could be predefined in relation to a topic cluster and were included in the final analysis. Nearly half of all 14,284 predefined messages addressed administrative issues, including 4166 (29.2%) scheduling-related inquiries, 1352 (9.5%) pharmacy and medication refill requests, and 581 (4.1%) insurance document issues. Among clinical concerns, of the total 14,284 predefined messages, 2975 (20.8%) messages involved vision disturbances, 1241 (8.7%) involved glaucoma-related symptoms, 1074 (7.5%) involved tumor-related questions, and 1064 (7.4%) involved surgery-relevant concerns. Message content differed significantly by demographic characteristics. Non-White patients more frequently raised issues related to pharmacy refills, insurance, glaucoma, and disability documentation, whereas White patients more often reported surgical concerns. Older patients more frequently messaged about glaucoma, surgery, and tumor-related issues, while female patients more often reported complications and swelling or infection. Conclusions: Secure patient messages frequently include clinically relevant symptoms with potential triage implications and demonstrate demographic differences in care-seeking behavior. Systematic analysis of message content may support safer triage, improved workflow efficiency, and more equitable delivery of ophthalmic care.
title: Secure Patient Messaging in Ophthalmology: Retrospective Natural Language Processing Study

summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as conversational agents for communication and guidance, but their ability to adapt responses to a patient’s emotional state and literacy level remains insufficiently characterized. In patient-facing scenarios, effective communication requires not only accurate medical content but also appropriate tone, clarity, and responsiveness to user vulnerability. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate, within a controlled, single-scenario experimental design, the ability of contemporary LLMs to adapt medical guidance responses to different levels of emotional sensitivity and literacy, and to assess their consistency in both generating and interpreting such adaptations. Methods: A controlled benchmark was designed to evaluate how 4 LLMs adapt medical guidance responses to predefined emotional and literacy levels for a realistic patient profile asking an open-ended question. To establish a robust performance baseline, one model was deployed locally (Gemma 3 27B), and 3 are cloud-based (Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT 5.2). Each model was tested across all combinations of 5 emotional levels, 3 literacy levels, and 3 prompt-verbosity variants, yielding 45 responses per model. Generated responses were assessed against human-reviewed ground truth for emotional and literacy alignment. A separate self-evaluation procedure measured each model’s ability to interpret its own outputs using the same adaptation framework. The study also examined generation-interpretation consistency and quantitative text properties, with particular attention to response length and verbosity. Results: Literacy adaptation was consistently accurate across models, often achieving near-zero error, indicating strong capability in adjusting explanatory complexity. In contrast, emotional adaptation showed greater variability and was more sensitive to model architecture and prompt design. The larger cloud-based models demonstrated more stable performance overall, while the local model exhibited higher variability, particularly under shorter prompts. A systematic asymmetry was observed between generation and interpretation. The models frequently misclassified low emotional and literacy levels as “normal,” suggesting limitations in recognizing user needs. Quantitative analysis revealed that response length increased with both emotional sensitivity and literacy level, with prompt verbosity and model-specific tendencies acting as secondary factors. Conclusions: Within our scenario, current LLMs demonstrated the capacity to support adaptive medical guidance, but their performance was uneven across dimensions, especially in terms of emotional generation and interpretation. For health care applications, these systems should be treated as assistive tools under human oversight rather than as autonomous communicators, with careful consideration of ethical, privacy, and safety implications in sensitive health contexts. title: Emotional and Literacy Adaptation in Large Language Model–Based Medical Guidance: Development and Usability Study

summary: Background: Medical record quality is a key focus of health care quality management. Traditional manual medical record quality control (QC) suffers from low efficiency, inability to achieve full-sample coverage, and poor consistency. Existing intelligent QC systems have significant deficiencies in real-time intervention and quantitative assessment of application effects. Objective: This study aimed to describe the design and development of the medical record quality control system (MRQCS) and to retrospectively evaluate its associations with medical record defect detection, medical record quality, and interreviewer consistency using 7-year longitudinal final-stage QC records (2019-2025). Methods: MRQCS implements a 2-level QC process for clinicians: nonblocking real-time prompting during documentation and blocking validation upon medical record completion. For QC reviewers, it provides AI-assisted defect detection and a 1-click write-back function. QC records from January 2019 to December 2025 were analyzed as 84 monthly discharge cohorts (43,324 sampled admissions), using interrupted time series (ITS) segmented regression with breakpoints aligned to the first discharge cohorts affected by each intervention (December 2020, July 2023, and May 2025). A stable‑rule‑set analysis was performed for genuine quality improvement. Linear mixed‑effects modeling with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) was applied to assess reviewer consistency, alongside multiple sensitivity analyses. Results: By 2025, the MRQCS QC rule library expanded from 41 rules initially to 597 rules. The sampled-case defect rate increased sharply after the January 2021 launch (trend change +0.06, 95% CI 0.03-0.08, P<.001), and rrates based on the 41 stable rules present in every year rose from 16.7% (880/5256) in 2021 to 50.9% (3662/7190) in 2023, indicating that most of the increase reflected improved system sensitivity. The high-risk case rate declined significantly after July 2023 (trend change –0.09, 95% CI –0.15 to –0.02, P=.007), and the residual defect rate showed an immediate decline at the May 2025 breakpoint (level change –0.44, 95% CI –0.85 to –0.03, P=.03). The AI-assisted write-back rate exceeded 97% after August 2023 and declined to 84%-87% after the May 2025 discharge blocking intervention (level change –2.14, 95% CI –3.08 to –1.21, P<.001), suggesting that clinicians corrected an increasing proportion of defects. Reviewer-level defect rates were far more homogeneous in the AI-assisted period (coefficient of variation [CV] 26.8% vs 115.7%), with reviewer identity accounting for a smaller share of the total variance (ICC 0.317 vs 0.782), indicating greater interreviewer consistency. Consistency of the high-risk defect rate showed the same pattern (CV 31.3% vs 135.3%; ICC 0.053 vs 0.541). Conclusions: Through the collaborative model of 2-level real-time QC and AI-assisted final-stage QC, MRQCS was associated with improved defect detection, reduction of documentation defects, and substantially greater interreviewer consistency; the discharge-time blocking intervention further reduced the residual defect rate. These findings provide a practical reference for the construction of medical record quality management systems.
title: Real-Time Medical Record Quality Control System (MRQCS): Development and Retrospective Longitudinal Observational Study
Clinical Readiness of Vital Sign–Based Sepsis Prediction

summary: Background: The Functional Independence Measure (FIM) is a standard functional assessment tool in rehabilitation medicine; however, formal assessments are often conducted only at limited intervals. Free-text clinical notes contain more frequent observations of patients’ functional status and may complement these assessments. Objective: This study aimed to estimate item-level FIM scores from Japanese free-text rehabilitation notes using a locally deployed large language model (LLM) and to evaluate estimation performance; item-level estimability; and differences across diseases, therapy types, and admission FIM severity groups. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed free-text notes from physical therapy (PT), occupational therapy (OT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) for patients hospitalized with cerebral infarction (CeI), hip fracture (HF), or vertebral fracture (VBF) at Saiseikai Moriyama Municipal Hospital between October 2019 and September 2024. Using zero-shot prompting, an LLM estimated all FIM items from each note. Estimated scores were matched to reference FIM scores recorded for the same patient on the same calendar date. Performance was evaluated using the mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error, and quadratic weighted kappa. Estimation rates and comparisons with modal-score and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) baselines were also examined. Results: Among 2,952,702 eligible note-item pairs from 164,039 retained rehabilitation-note-level outputs, the model produced 980,000 valid estimates, corresponding to an overall estimation rate of 33.2%. Among 170,744 note-item opportunities with an available same-day reference score, 57,246 (33.5%) were estimable, of which 77.7% (44,481/57,246) were within 1 point of the reference score. Estimates derived from OT notes had a lower MAE than those derived from PT notes in CeI and HF, whereas the difference was not significant in VBF. The LLM outperformed the modal-score baseline but had a higher MAE than the LOCF overall (0.825 vs 0.648). Conclusions: The locally deployed LLM shows the potential to derive item-level FIM estimates from Japanese rehabilitation notes. Among estimable note-item pairs with a same-day reference FIM score, 77.7% were within 1 point of the reference score. These findings support the potential use of LLM-based estimation to structure functional information contained in routine rehabilitation notes and complement periodic FIM assessments. Further integration of multidisciplinary clinical records and external validation are needed to improve estimability and evaluate its value for longitudinal functional monitoring.
title: Estimating Functional Independence Measure Scores From Japanese Rehabilitation Notes Using a Large Language Model: Retrospective Study

summary: Ambient AI scribes have been rapidly adopted across health care organizations to mitigate documentation burden and burnout. Initial single-system reports described substantial time savings, but more recent multisite evaluations and meta-analyses describe modest, heterogeneous effects with generally low methodological quality. Most evaluations emphasize efficiency and satisfaction, leaving potential effects on communication quality, narrative preservation, cognitive performance, and equity largely unmeasured. This viewpoint aimed to characterize evaluation patterns in prominent ambient AI scribe implementations, explain why unmeasured domains warrant investigation for patient safety and care quality, and propose an expanded framework with feasible research priorities. This analytic viewpoint mapped evaluation domain coverage in a purposive, illustrative sample of prominent implementation reports published through April 2026, then synthesized findings with literature on clinical communication, narrative medicine, automation effects, and health equity. Reporting was guided by Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) principles for narrative reviews; PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) was not used because the work is a domain-coverage characterization rather than an evidence synthesis estimating effects. A single reviewer (VSME) performed selection and extraction, consistent with the viewpoint’s illustrative intent. Across the included implementations, evaluation consistently measured documentation time, after-hours work, and clinician satisfaction. Within this illustrative sample of 6 independently peer-reviewed real-world implementation evaluations, we did not identify any that reported systematic assessment of patient-clinician communication using validated instruments, structured comparison of AI-generated against human-generated notes for narrative fidelity, longitudinal evaluation of cognitive or educational effects, or equity analyses stratified by language and demographic group. The absence in this purposive sample reflects an absence of public reporting rather than proof that no organization has measured these dimensions internally. Limited error analyses found frequent omissions, with accuracy declining as encounter complexity increased. Evidence from multilingual and interpreter-mediated encounters was notably sparse. Current evidence supports continued implementation with quality safeguards in settings where benefits are demonstrated locally rather than universal adoption on the strength of early single-system reports. Organizations implementing ambient AI scribes should consider embedding prospective evaluation across 4 domains: validated communication quality measurement, structured narrative content comparison, longitudinal cognitive and training studies, and equity analyses across languages and demographics. Three near-term priorities offer immediate feasibility for organizations with evaluation capacity: (1) deploying validated communication instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool or Consumer Assessment of Health Care Providers and Systems (CAHPS) within ongoing rollouts; (2) launching multisite longitudinal trainee cohorts comparing programs with and without ambient AI exposure; and (3) oversampling multilingual and interpreter-mediated encounters for stratified equity analyses. Narrative preservation requires foundational methodological work before implementation-ready measures exist. Editors, implementers, and vendors can each act now: editors by requiring domain-coverage reporting; implementers by preregistering evaluation plans before rollout; vendors by publishing stratified performance data as a routine condition of deployment. The goal is to preserve documented efficiency gains while generating evidence about communication, narrative, reasoning, and equity dimensions that current evaluations leave unmeasured.
title: Beyond Time Saved: A Framework for Comprehensive Evaluation of AI Clinical Documentation

summary: Background: Publicly accessible, internet-based AI chatbots have emerged as unregulated digital health resources that clinicians and patients consult in real time, including during acute medical emergencies. In dental practice—where life-threatening events such as anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, and severe hypoglycemia can unfold within seconds—the unsupervised use of these tools as point-of-care decision aids poses uncharacterized patient safety risks. Despite widespread deployment, no study has systematically evaluated the accuracy, temporal consistency, or multilingual reliability of contemporary large language model (LLM)–based chatbots specifically for dental medical emergency management. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the accuracy, temporal stability, and multilingual performance of five contemporary LLM-based chatbots when queried on the management of medical emergencies in dental practice. Methods: A comparative study was conducted to assess five AI chatbots: ChatGPT-5.2 (OpenAI), Gemini 3.1 (Google), DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek AI), Grok 4.20 (xAI), and Kimi K2.5 (Moonshot AI). A total of 130 questions covering dental medical emergency management were developed and categorized into four formats: multiple-choice questions (MCQs), yes-or-no questions, open-ended WH questions, and clinical scenario questions. Each question was presented using two prompting strategies (basic and advanced) across three languages (English, Arabic, and Chinese). Data collection was performed over seven consecutive days, generating 27,300 chatbot responses. Responses were evaluated by language-specific expert reviewers and classified as correct or incorrect based on established clinical references. Statistical analysis was performed using chi-square tests to assess associations between accuracy and study variables. Pairwise post hoc comparisons of column proportions were conducted using z-tests with Bonferroni correction. Results: A total of 27,300 responses were analyzed; 25,377 (92.96%) were correct. Question type significantly influenced chatbot performance (<.001), with MCQs demonstrating the highest accuracy (5942/6300, 94.3%), and WH questions demonstrating the lowest accuracy (7686/8400, 91.5%). Language also showed a significant association with accuracy (=.01), with English prompts achieving the highest accuracy (8512/9100, 93.5%). Chatbot model performance differed significantly (<.001), with Gemini 3.1 demonstrating the highest accuracy (5176/5460, 94.8%; 95% CI 94.21%‐95.39%), followed by ChatGPT-5.2 (5105/5460, 93.5%; 95% CI 92.85%‐94.15%) and Kimi K2.5 (5071/5460, 92.9%). Prompt complexity and testing day did not significantly affect response accuracy (=.69 and =.96, respectively). Conclusions: Current LLM-based chatbots demonstrate high accuracy in answering structured questions related to dental medical emergency management. However, performance varies according to question format and language, and the presence of incorrect responses highlights potential safety concerns. AI chatbots may serve as educational tools, but their use as real-time decision support during dental medical emergencies should be approached with caution.
title: Evaluating Internet-Based AI Chatbots as Unregulated Digital Health Resources in Dental Emergency Management: Comparative Multilingual Study

summary: Background: With the rapid expansion of health care data, multiple international standardized terminology systems have been developed and refined to ensure semantic interoperability, which is a crucial factor in facilitating collaborative use. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the real-world use and applicability of standardized terminology systems by mapping clinical terms from routine cancer care and to propose guidelines that optimize mapping. Methods: Clinical terms generated during cancer care at the National Cancer Center Korea were extracted and mapped to multiple target terminology systems: the Korean Standard Classification of Diseases; ; Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes; RxNorm; Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification; and Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms (SNOMED CT). A multidisciplinary working group of health care information managers, data experts, and oncologists verified the mapping outcomes, calculated the cross-verification discordance rate, and compared the coverage across systems. Results: A total of 3472 source terms were identified across 7 domains: chief complaint, diagnosis, laboratory test, imaging test, surgery/procedure, medication, and radiation therapy. With postcoordination and predefined mapping guidelines, SNOMED CT achieved high overall mapping rates (98.3%‐100%) across domains. Applying postcoordination as needed substantially improved exact semantic match rates, which exceeded 90% in most domains. However, more than 40% of source terms were broadly mapped in the imaging test and radiation therapy domains because procedural details such as imaging technique and radiation field configuration could not be represented in SNOMED CT. The cross-verification discordance rate between mappers, defined as the proportion of source terms with disagreement, remained low (0.3%‐1.3%). RxNorm and Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes showed complementary strengths within their specialized domains, adding detail or specificity where SNOMED CT was less complete. Conclusions: Standardized terminology systems are feasible and effective in encoding clinical terms for cancer care. SNOMED CT was the most comprehensive, and predefined mapping guidelines provide a structured framework for mapping and consensus resolution. Domain-specific systems should be used alongside SNOMED CT, and all systems should be updated regularly to reflect evolving clinical practice.
title: Real-World Applicability of Multiple International Terminology Systems in Oncology: Mapping Study of Clinical Terms for Cancer Diagnosis and Treatment
